query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In an initially single‐phase high-entropy alloy, exposure to low temperature coupled with high strain-rate deformation drives localized, deformation-induced elemental segregation at grain boundaries. This segregated boundary acts as a weak link that promotes brittle (often intergranular) failure, whereas deformation at higher temperatures or lower strain rates allows sufficient dislocation mobility to mitigate segregation and preserve ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: A single‐phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy (e.g., refractory HEA such as MoNbTaTiV) with a uniform elemental distribution.
generation.intervention: Conduct mechanical deformation tests under controlled conditions by varying temperature and strain rate; specifically compare tests at low temperature/high strain rate versus high temperature/low strain rate.
generation.conditions: Same alloy composition subjected to two regimes: one that favors restricted atomic mobility (low temperature, high strain rate) and one allowing enhanced dislocation-mediated homogenization (high temperature, low strain rate), with all other processing parameters (including retention of a single-phase microstructure) kept constant.
generation.structural_mediator: Localized grain boundary segregation of certain alloying elements induced under aggressive deformation conditions.
generation.mechanism: Under low temperature and high strain rate, dislocation movement is insufficient to uniformly redistribute atoms. This causes certain elements to cluster at the grain boundaries, reducing local cohesive strength. In contrast, at higher temperatures or lower strain rates, enhanced dislocation mobility prevents or reverses segregation, resulting in more ductile, transgranular failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under low temperature/high strain rate conditions, microscopic analysis should reveal enhanced elemental segregation at the grain boundaries with a correlated shift toward intergranular (brittle) fracture, compared to high temperature/low strain rate conditions that retain a more homogeneous boundary composition and ductile fracture behavior.
generation.baseline: The single-phase HEA in its as-sintered or as-cast state, exhibiting homogeneous composition and ductile transgranular fracture under moderate deformation conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to deformation regimes typical of high-temperature service in which the high-entropy alloy avoids deleterious intermetallic phases. It is limited to conditions where the primary microstructural change is deformation-induced segregation rather than transformation to multiphase structures.
generation.uncertainty: The exact strain rate and temperature thresholds for the onset of significant grain boundary segregation remain to be precisely determined, and the influence of subtle grain-boundary morphology changes (e.g., serration) on mitigating or exacerbating the effect is not fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical samples of the high-entropy alloy and divide them into two groups. Subject one group to low temperature/high strain rate deformation and the other group to high temperature/low strain rate deformation. Use high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM) combined with energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) to characterize the grain boundary chemistry, and perform fractographic analysis to identify fracture modes.
measurements: Grain boundary elemental distribution (via TEM/EDS mapping)
Fracture surface analysis (intergranular vs. transgranular features)
Mechanical properties: tensile ductility, toughness, and fracture strain
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If low temperature/high strain rate conditions do not produce a statistically significant increase in grain boundary segregation relative to the baseline or if the fracture mode remains predominantly ductile (i.e., transgranular) rather than brittle (intergranular), then the hypothesis that deformation-induced segregation mediates toughness degradation in the HEA would be falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractA powder-metallurgy MoNbTaTiV refractory high-entropy alloy synthesized by mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering was subjected to hot deformations at different temperatures and strain rates. The microstructural morphologies were characterized, and component element segregation was elucidated. With grain refinement and lattice strain increase, the large inhomogeneous milled powder became refined and homogeneous after the MA. Component element segregation was observed at relatively low deformation temperatures and high strain rates. As the deformation temperature increased and the strain rate decreased, the segregation gradually disappeared, which was attributed to dislocation movement.Keywords: Refractory high-entropy alloy, Mechanical alloying, Segregation, Hot deformation, Microstructure Highlights•A powder-metallurgy MoNbTaTiV RHEA was synthesized by mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering.•The deformation-induced component element segregation in the refractory high-entropy alloy was elucidated.•Effects of deformation temperature and strain rate on the deformation-induced grain boundary segregation were obtained.

ABSTRACTIn this study, tensile and creep deformation of a high-entropy alloy processed by selective laser melting (SLM) has been investigated; hot ductility drop was identified at first, and the loss of ductility at elevated temperature was associated with intergranular fracture. By modifying the grain boundary morphology from straight to serration, the hot ductility drop issue has been resolved successfully. The serrated grain boundary could be achieved by reducing the cooling rate of solution heat treatment, which allowed the coarsening of L12 structured γ′ precipitates to interfere with mobile grain boundaries, resulting in undulation of the grain boundary morphology. Tensile and creep tests at 650°C were conducted, and serrated grain boundary could render a significant increase in tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life by a factor of 3.5 and 400, respectively. Detailed microstructure analysis has indicated that serrated grain boundary could distribute strains more evenly than that of straight morphology.
